rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and makes the reporter's verification work obvious. Its strongest line, "Oatly's reformulated barista blend cuts climate footprint 31% per liter, verified by third-party LCA," is a real beat-shaped hook with the exact proof a climate reporter would demand. B has useful instincts, but "customers who don't specify get oat milk" turns "default non-dairy option" into a different claim entirely, and that is how a pitch gets deleted with prejudice.
gaps_in_A: "Oatly wins its biggest pour-volume deal" invents "biggest"; the update gives 1,400 locations, not Oatly's largest deal or volume.
"in the same quarter it closes a US plant" is over-specific; the update says the loss was last quarter and the plant is closing, not that all events sit in the same quarter.
The partnership angle includes "no price change at retail," which is a retail fact awkwardly bolted onto a foodservice story.
gaps_in_B: "customers who don't specify get oat milk" misreads the update. The fact says Oatly becomes the default non-dairy option, not the default milk for every unspecified order.
"falling volumes, shrinking retail shelf space, canceled expansions" is invented category scenery. None of that appears in the update.
"surviving brands are choosing depth over breadth" is a thesis pretending to be evidence. One Oatly plant closure plus one chain deal does not prove a sector strategy.

It keeps "Northeast coffee chain makes oat milk the default" while refusing "Customer-story (the coffee chain's procurement decision)" because the chain is unnamed. Pick a lane; contradiction is not rigor.
